title: Agents That Go Looking for Work
description: Ten tools where the agent handles the outreach, the applications or the inbox: job search, Instagram and Telegram leads, ASO, helpdesk and forms.
content:
# Agents That Go Looking for Work

There is a category of AI tool that does not help you write anything. It finds the thing that needs doing, does the first pass, and hands you a decision.

That is a more valuable category than it sounds. The bottleneck in most knowledge work is not producing text; it is noticing that something is waiting, and then doing the same small task for the fortieth time.

## Money you forgot about

[[link:/tools/2248|Qovilio]] is the clearest example of the pattern. Forward a billing email to your own Qovilio address, drop a PDF or photo of a receipt, or import a CSV from your old tracker, and every subscription, renewal and trial lands in one view. You can also just ask it what renews this week or what you spend on AI tools, and every change is undoable. Three input routes means no manual entry, which is the only reason a tracker like this survives past week two.

## Being named when the question is asked

[[link:/tools/2249|AI Knows Us]] works on a problem most people have not noticed yet: when a buyer asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity who to use, three to five businesses get named, and if you are not one of them you never hear about the deal. The service finds the questions your buyers actually ask — with your name deliberately excluded so the answers stay honest — shows who gets named and which pages the AI trusted, then publishes answer-first pages built to be quoted and re-checks on a schedule.

What makes it credible is the evidence. The site publishes its own Search Console exports, including a domain that went from five impressions a day to 2,685 in nine days, and states plainly that rates come with a range so you see movement rather than noise.

## Proving a skill instead of listing it

[[link:/tools/2250|Spotlytt]] replaces the resume screen with a role-specific AI interview. Questions adapt to your target role and experience, and your strongest answers become evidence: skill-by-skill scores, short video clips, and a public profile with a job-readiness estimate and a gap analysis. Whether employers adopt it is an open question, but the underlying complaint — that a PDF cannot show how someone thinks — is real.

## Outreach, carefully

[[link:/tools/2251|OpenSparta]] is an AI agent for Telegram: it finds relevant conversations, writes contextual comments, and manages accounts and proxies from one workspace, using official client protocols with per-account safety limits and FloodWait quarantine. The honesty is unusual — automated commenting carries genuine platform risk, and the product says so rather than pretending otherwise.

[[link:/tools/2252|Ins Autopilot]] takes the same job to Instagram, but runs inside your own signed-in Chrome session, so no password is ever required. It surfaces contacts from followers, likers and commenters, keeps notes and message history per account locally, and with Pro drafts DMs using your own provider key and runs follow-up sequences that stop when a reply arrives.

[[link:/tools/2253|FreeApply]] is the most disciplined of the three. It runs through the AI app you already use — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or Windsurf — searches the job sites you pick, fills in applications with your real details, and refuses to invent experience: anything a cover letter cannot back up is declined and it asks you instead. About 90 KB, and your resume stays on your computer.

[[link:/tools/2254|Winch]] is App Store optimization run by your own agent. It tracks keywords in 175 countries across both stores, rewrites listings in every language, draws store art, and lets the agent answer in plain words or drive the interface itself. One-time $69 licence, and it runs on the Claude, ChatGPT or OpenRouter plan you already pay for.

## The queues you already have

[[link:/tools/2255|OpenDesk]] is an Apache-2.0 helpdesk where support email, live chat, your help centre and your team's own mail accounts land in one queue, and Ollie drafts replies in any language. Free for one mailbox in the cloud, or self-host in one command. It is the open-source answer to Zendesk pricing, and it takes privacy seriously enough to be worth the setup.

[[link:/tools/2256|Formstep]] attacks the form rather than the inbox. Each request is a one-person form with values you already know prefilled and locked, so the recipient answers without making an account, and an AI validation checks an upload against what was claimed before it reaches you. Responses route into n8n, Zapier, Claude or ChatGPT, and it is hosted in the EU.

[[link:/tools/2257|Squint]] is the smallest tool here and possibly the most used. Press the hotkey, drag a box around whatever is confusing on your screen, and the answer streams in beside it. No screenshot, no tab switch, no describing what you are looking at. Follow-ups happen in the same panel, and it runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

## The common shape

None of these tools writes your emails for you in a way you would publish. They remove a queue: the subscriptions you forgot, the buyers who never heard of you, the applications you did not send, the tickets waiting on a first reply, the form that needs three follow-up emails.

[[link:/tools/2253|FreeApply]] refusing to invent experience and [[link:/tools/2252|Ins Autopilot]] telling you it cannot guarantee account safety are the two most encouraging details in this group. Both are choosing to be less impressive and more trustworthy, which is the right trade for a tool that acts on your behalf.

If you adopt one, start with the queue you dread most. That is where an agent earns its place.
tldr: Qovilio, AI Knows Us, Spotlytt, OpenSparta, Ins Autopilot, FreeApply, Winch, OpenDesk, Formstep and Squint all remove a queue of small decisions rather than writing prose for you.
